t66a_fg1p3w10p1: They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay, and in theory they could have done something else. It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. Maybe you've decided you're never speaking to them again. That can still be the right call, and so can a boundary, or the law, or saying out loud that it was wrong. None of it rules out forgiving them someday. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."

t66a_fg1p1w10p1: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can't be put on a schedule (nobody gets a gold star for forgiving fastest). And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Resentment does narrow what you see, though, and it keeps your little one organized around the injury. But pushed early, forgiveness turns into a performance, all peace on the surface, while the wound goes underground.
t66a_fg1p1w11p1: Maybe you've heard "You have to forgive to heal." For many people healing does come to include some forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. It just can't be put on a schedule, and it isn't the price of anything else: you can get safe without it, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice and recover. Resentment narrows what you see and keeps your little one organized around the injury. But forgive early because you're told to, and you get the enlightened version ("I've made my peace") while the wound goes underground.
t66a_fg1p1w12p1: Forgiveness, for a lot of people, does come eventually, or at least they stop living under the resentment. Not on a schedule, though. And you don't need it first. What can help is seeing how they got there. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay, and in theory they could have done something else. It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. Maybe you've decided you're never speaking to them again. That can still be the right call, and so can a boundary, or the law, or saying out loud that it was wrong. None of it rules out forgiving them someday. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."
